title: ANIME WORKOUTS - Can you build superhuman grip strength like Hanayama from Grappler Baki
summary: Using Hanayama (Baki) and Reito (Kengan Ashura) as hooks, NH explains the three grip types, support, pinch and crush, and how to train each for strength and forearm size. He gives exercise lists, volume and frequency guidelines, and argues for straps on heavy pulls plus frequent dedicated grip work.
claims: Grip strength is the expression of strength that draws him most; it is widely depicted in fighting manga as power fantasy
Hanayama and Reito were born with their strength, but because those are exaggerated human traits they can be developed
Grip training grows the forearms, though less directly than people think
There are three grip types (support, pinch, crush); training only one leaves incomplete development
Relying only on heavy deadlifts and rows for grip lets a small muscle limit back work and makes grip fatigue hard to track, leading to under-recovery
Use straps on heavy deadlifts, rows and shrugs to save grip for dedicated forearm work; grip the bar on warm-ups
Support grip builds size because the load stretches the forearm fibers, causing muscle damage
Support grip carries over to every other grip type; the limiting factor of grip is usually the hands, not the forearms
For grip-specific heavy holds, use shrugs or above-the-knee rack pulls for time
Coan grip suitcase hold: 3-4 sets of 15 s per arm; add 5 lb when easy
Towel through a plate, deadlifted and held for time, changes wrist angle and involves the fingers more
Include elbow and wrist flexion (reverse curls, wrist curls) to develop the full forearm and brachioradialis via dynamic re-gripping
All support grip variations (pull-ups, hangs, rows, shrugs, curls, rack pulls, towel holds) help and should be used to some degree
Anyone who says deadlifts are all you need for grip and forearms is an idiot
Pinch grip increases finger contact and reduces palm contact; thicker implements prevent locking the thumb
Finger curls give a strong forearm stretch and build support grip but aren't pinch grip
Thick bars or fat grips train pinch grip but reduce the weight you can move, hurting the movement's target muscles
Loading pins let you attach many pinch implements and progressively overload easily; climbing boards also train fingers
Don't buy every grip gadget; pick a few key movements per grip type and push progression
Crush grip is the least important because it gives the forearms no stretch, with little carryover
Train crush grip with grippers (he recommends Captains of Crush) 3-4x/week, 4-8 sets of 4-15 reps; move up when you hit 10 reps easily
Train support and pinch grip at least 4x/week at varying intensities; low frequency is the enemy of forearm development
Forearms and hands lack work capacity but recover fast, so they suit supersets and fit anywhere in a program
Avoid mixed or hook grip on grip exercises
Finger push-ups strengthen fingers but won't build forearms
Farmer walks build grip, forearms and yoke together
Specialized support grip holds: beginners 3 sets/week of 5-15 s, progressing to 8 sets/week
Specialized elbow/wrist flexion: beginners 4 sets/week of 6-10 reps, progressing to 8-12 sets/week of 8-12 reps
Pinch grip work is a subset of support grip, so subtract it from support volume and rotate styles often
Grippers: beginners 8 sets/week of 4-15 reps over 2 sessions, progressing to 16-20 sets/week
exercises: barbell held at the side like a suitcase, 3-4x15 s per arm, +5 lb
overloads grip with only forearms limiting

let bar roll to fingertips then curl
